preserved_objections.basis: Wavelet decomposition is fundamentally designed for time-frequency analysis of signals with stationary or cyclical patterns, but retail demand data contains multiple non-stationary components (promotions, holidays, assortment changes) that wavelets cannot properly isolate, as shown by the absence of wavelet-based approaches in the provided evidence which focuses on LSTM, SVR, and meta-learning techniques

The candidate fails to define boundary conditions for handling multi-dimensional retail data (product hierarchies, store clusters, external factors) where wavelet decomposition would require complex extensions that are not specified, making the approach impractical for real-world retail environments with thousands of SKUs across multiple stores

None of the provided evidence references wavelet decomposition for demand forecasting; instead, all citations focus on LSTM networks, SVR models, meta-learning approaches, and federated learning, contradicting the candidate's proposed mechanism and suggesting no empirical support exists for this approach in retail forecasting

The candidate provides no theoretical or empirical basis for why wavelet features would outperform raw features in detecting drift, and the testable prediction only compares detection time without establishing that the wavelet approach would actually improve forecast accuracy or reduce stockouts compared to the baseline

Wavelet decomposition requires selecting appropriate wavelet families and decomposition levels, which is non-trivial for retail data with multiple seasonal patterns, and the candidate provides no methodology for making these critical decisions, making implementation impossible without extensive additional research

The testable prediction fails to define what constitutes "significant changes" in decomposed feature components, how these changes will be quantified, or what thresholds would trigger drift detection, rendering the measurement ambiguous and the prediction untestable as specified
